Emulsion Presets — full catalog

451 open-source film emulation and creative presets for Adobe Lightroom and Camera Raw.
MIT licensed. Free. No paywall. Each preset is a standalone .xmp file.
Repository: https://github.com/peva3/EmulsionPresets

Color Negative Film (83 presets)
C-41 negative film emulations: Kodak Portra, Gold, Ektar, Ultramax, Fuji Superia, Pro, Reala, cinema stocks.

- Adox Color Implosion (Color): Adox Color Implosion was a deliberately flawed experimental color negative film produced by Adox (Fotoimpex, Germany).
- Agfa Optima 100 (Color): Agfa Optima 100 was a German consumer-grade color negative film produced from the mid-1990s through the mid-2000s.
- Agfa Optima 200 (Color): Agfa Optima 200 was the faster variant of the Agfa Optima consumer color negative family. Produced from the mid-1990s through the mid-2000s.
- Agfa Ultra 100 (Color): High saturation consumer film, vibrant reds, warm yellow cast, discontinued 2005
- Agfa Vista 100 (Color): Budget color negative, neutral palette, fine grain for price point
- Agfa Vista 200 (Color): Everyday 200-speed consumer film, natural skin tones, balanced rendering
- Agfa Vista 400 (Color): High-speed budget film, moderate grain, warm rendering, all-rounder
- C Print (Color): RA-4 chromogenic color paper character, soft contrast, pastel shadow tones
- CineStill 400D (Color): Daylight-balanced cinema film, remjet removed, halation glow in highlights
- CineStill 50D (Color): Daylight-balanced color negative cinema film (remjet removed)
- Ferrania Solaris FG 400 (Color): Italian 400-speed, grain-heavy rendering, warm Mediterranean color palette
- Fuji 100 Industrial (Color): Japanese-market-only consumer film, ultra-fine grain, cool-neutral balance. Known as the "Japanese Superia." Sold in bulk in Japan as "Fujicolor 100 Industrial".
- Fuji NPS 160 Pulled (Color): Fujicolor NPS 160 pulled 1 stop (overexposed + reduced development). Low contrast, low saturation, cooler color balance, finer grain, soft contrast portrait film.
- Fuji Natura 1600 (Color): Japanese-market high-speed color negative, designed for Fuji Natura Classica, NP mode
- Fuji Pro 160C (Color): Higher-contrast, higher-saturation professional color negative. The "vivid" sibling in Fujifilm's PRO 160 line.
- Fuji Pro 160NS (Color): The definitive breakdown of Fujifilm's pastel portrait film — cool-cyan shadows, low contrast, and the "pro wedding photographer" palette.
- Fuji Pro 800Z (Color): High-speed professional portrait film. Fujifilm's answer to Portra 800 — warm tones, moderate grain, low-light mastery.
- Fuji Reala 100 (Color): Fourth color layer for accurate greens, neutral skin tones, archival-grade, discontinued
- Fuji Superia 100 (Color): Fine-grain consumer film, cool-neutral color, sharp acutance, entry-level quality
- Fuji Superia 1600 (Color): High-speed consumer negative, prominent grain, cool shadow cast, low-light option
- Fuji Superia 200 (Color): General purpose 200-speed, slightly cool bias, good skin, reliable all-rounder
- Fuji Superia 800 (Color): Fast consumer film, punchy saturation, green-leaning shadow tones
- Fuji Superia HG 1600 (Color): "High Grade" Superia variant — premium high-speed consumer film. Finer grain than standard Superia 1600, better skin tones, less green shadow cast.
- Fuji Superia X-TRA 400 +1 (Color): Overexposed 1 stop, pastel rendering, reduced grain, softer contrast
- Fuji Superia X-TRA 400 (Color): Versatile consumer 400-speed, punchy greens, cool-leaning shadow tones
- Fujicolor C200 (Color): Entry-level 200-speed, warm-golden bias, decent exposure latitude
- Fujicolor NPH (Color): Professional portrait/wedding film, low contrast, neutral skin tones, Pro 400H precursor
- Fujicolor Superia Premium 400 (Color): Japanese-market premium 400-speed, finer grain than standard Superia X-TRA
- Fujifilm Classic Chrome (Color): A complete analysis of the Classic Chrome look: color palette, contrast behavior, tonal response, and how it differs from other Fujifilm simulations.
- Fujifilm Classic Negative (Color): Soft magenta-yellow palette, muted saturation, raised blacks, nostalgic digital simulation
- Fujifilm Pro 400H (Color): The definitive breakdown of the "400H look" — why wedding photographers and editorial shooters are still grieving.
- Fujifilm Eterna (Color): Primary: Soft, muted, low-contrast cinematic look with warm cast
- Fujifilm Nostalgic Negative (Color): Digital film simulation (Fujifilm X-T5 / X-Trans V)
- Kodacolor VR 200 (Color): 1980s consumer negative, warm-yellow cast, moderate grain, vintage snapshots
- Kodak ColorPlus 200 (Color): Budget consumer film, warm yellow-red bias, high latitude, very forgiving
- Kodak Ektar 100 +1 (Color): Overexposed Ektar, slightly softer saturation, creamier skin tones than box speed
- Kodak Ektar 100 (Color): Tagline: "Slide film in C-41 clothing" — Ultra-saturated color negative with minimal grain, high contrast, and warm earth tones. A polarizing film stock that either delights or overwhelms.
- Kodak Farbwelt 200 Expired (Color): European-market Kodak variant, 10+ year expired, magenta-shifted color, faded contrast
- Kodak Gold 200 +1 (Color): Overexposed Gold 200, pastel-soft contrast, dreamy highlight blooming
- Kodak Gold 200 +2 (Color): Overexposed 2 stops, very pastel, washed-out sun-bleached snapshot aesthetic
- Kodak Gold 200 Expired 10yr (Color): 10-year expired Gold, slight magenta color shift, reduced contrast from age
- Kodak Gold 200 Expired 30yr (Color): 30-year expired, heavy magenta-green shift, pronounced grain, extreme color cast
- Kodak Gold 200 Frontier (Color): Frontier SP3000 lab scan, high contrast, vibrant Kodak yellow rendering
- Kodak Gold 200 Noritsu (Color): Noritsu HS-1800 lab scan, softer contrast, greener shadow balance
- Kodak Gold 200 (Color): Warm golden consumer classic, punchy yellows, approachable contrast, every-shooter film
- Kodak High Definition Plus 200 (Color): Fine-grain 200-speed consumer emulsion, clean rendering, HD marketing era
- Kodak Max 800 (Color): High-speed consumer zoom-film, heavy grain, warm rendering, late-1990s era
- Kodak Portra 160 (Color): Ultra-soft contrast, wide dynamic range, pastel-flawless skin.
- Kodak Portra 160NC (Color): "Natural Color" — the lower-contrast, more neutral variant of Portra 160. The choice for accuracy-first commercial and fine art photographers.
- Kodak Portra 160VC (Color): Pre-2010 "Vivid Color" Portra variant. Higher saturation and contrast than standard Portra, less pastel. The bridal/fashion photographers' choice before the current unified Portra line.
- Kodak Portra 400 +1 (Color): Overexposed 1 stop, softer pastel palette, extended highlight detail on skin
- Kodak Portra 400 +2 (Color): Overexposed 2 stops, ethereal pastel rendering, airy skin tones, editorial look
- Kodak Portra 400 -1 (Color): Underexposed 1 stop, punchier contrast, slightly deeper saturation, grittier
- Kodak Portra 400 120 (Color): Medium format look, finer apparent grain, smoother tonality at 6x6/6x7
- Kodak Portra 400 4x5 (Color): Large format look, virtually grainless, maximum detail and dynamic range
- Kodak Portra 400 Expired (Color): Aged Portra stock, muted contrast, subtle color shift from emulsion aging
- Kodak Portra 400 Noritsu (Color): Noritsu lab scan profile, greener shadow balance, softer contrast rendering
- Kodak Portra 400 (Color): Everything that makes Portra 400 the most sought-after film stock for digital emulation. Warmer than 160, Noritsu vs Frontier, overexposure behavior, and the "scan vs negative" debate.
- Kodak Portra 400NC (Color): "Natural Color" at 400 speed — the most accurate, neutral 400-speed color negative film ever made. Discontinued in 2010.
- Kodak Portra 400UC (Color): "Ultra Color" / "Vivid Color" — Portra 400 with the saturation turned up. The choice for fashion, editorial, and vibrant commercial work.
- Kodak Portra 400VC (Color): Pre-2010 "Vivid Color" 400-speed Portra variant. Punchier than standard Portra 400, more contrast, warmer and more saturated skin tones. The higher-speed sibling of Portra 160VC.
- Kodak Portra 800 +1 (Color): Overexposed 800, cleaner shadows, reduced grain, softer contrast rendering
- Kodak Portra 800 -1 (Color): Underexposed 800, grittier grain structure, boosted contrast, low-light aesthetic
- Kodak Portra 800 (Color): High-speed professional portrait film, warm tones, moderate grain, low-light king
- Kodak Pro Image 100 (Color): Tropical-market prosumer film, warm skin, humidity-resistant, affordable professional
- Kodak Royal Gold 400 (Color): Discontinued premium consumer 400, rich saturation, finer grain than standard Gold
- Kodak Ultramax 400 +1 (Color): Overexposed Ultramax, softer yellow-blue rendering, reduced grain appearance
- Kodak Ultramax 400 +2 (Color): Heavily overexposed, flat pastel palette, sun-faded consumer film aesthetic
- Kodak Ultramax 400 (Color): Punchy all-rounder consumer film, warm yellow cast, high contrast, affordable 400
- Kodak Vericolor III 160 (Color): Professional portrait film (pre-1998). Extremely low contrast, very pastel, magenta-leaning shadows. The wedding and school portrait standard for 20+ years.
- Kodak Vericolor VPS (Color): ISO 160 color negative film, introduced 1979. Part of the Vericolor family. Even lower contrast than Vericolor III. "VPS" = Vericolor Print Slide.
- Kodak Vision3 250D ECN-2 (Color): Daylight cinema film stock, full ECN-2 process look, wide dynamic range
- Kodak Vision3 250D (Color): Cross-processed in C-41, remjet removed, classic cinematic halation glow
- Kodak Vision3 500T ECN-2 (Color): Tungsten cinema film stock, full ECN-2, incredible low-light cine latitude
- Kodak Vision3 500T (Color): Cross-processed in C-41, tungsten-to-daylight color shift, cinematic grain
- Kodak Vision3 50D (Color): Slow daylight cinema film, ultra-fine grain, saturated cinematic color
- Kodak Ektachrome 320T (Color): Tungsten-balanced color reversal (slide) film
- Lomochrome Purple (Color): Color-shift creative film, greens render as purple, surreal Lomo palette
- Lomography Color 100 (Color): Lomo's 100-speed negative, boosted saturation, vignette-heavy character
- ORWO NC 500 (Color): ORWO Wolfen NC 500 is a modern color negative film produced by ORWO (Original Wolfen) in Bitterfeld-Wolfen, Germany — the historic East German film factory.
- RA-4 Color Print (Color): RA-4 wet print emulation, paper base warmth, darkroom color print aesthetic
- Rollei Crossbird 200 (Color): Rollei Crossbird 200 is a specialty film intended for cross-processing — shooting slide (E-6) film and developing it in C-41 (color negative) chemistry.
- SantaColor Aerocolor (Color): Aerial survey film repurposed, fine grain, high sharpness, cool-neutral balance

Black & White Film (58 presets)
Monochrome emulations: Tri-X, T-Max, HP5, Delta, Pan F, Acros, Neopan, Fomapan, Rollei, Adox.

- Adox Silvermax 21 (Monochrome): Adox Silvermax 21 is an ultra-slow, ultra-fine-grain black-and-white negative film produced by Adox (Germany).
- Agfa APX 100 (Monochrome): Fine grain, wide exposure latitude, cool-neutral tonality, classic European B&W
- Agfa APX 25 (Monochrome): Ultra-fine grain, very high resolution, smooth gradation, discontinued gem
- Agfa APX 400 (Monochrome): Agfa APX 400 was the high-speed member of Agfa's classic APX black-and-white film family. Sitting above APX 25 and APX 100, it offered a versatile combination of speed, moderate grain.
- Agfa Scala 200 (Monochrome): B&W reversal (slide) film, deep blacks, high contrast, unique direct-positive
- Bergger Pancro 400 (Monochrome): Bergger Pancro 400 is a French-made black-and-white negative film produced by Bergger Products. Its defining innovation is a dual-emulsion coating: two separate emulsion layers.
- Copper Tone (Monochrome): Warm copper split-tone on monochrome base, metallic highlight sheen
- Dramatic Monochrome (Monochrome): High contrast, crushed blacks, intense dramatic mood, fine-art B&W punch
- Foma Fomapan 100 (Monochrome): Fomapan 100 is a classic cubic-grain black-and-white negative film produced by Foma Bohemia (Hradec Kralove, Czech Republic).
- Foma Fomapan 200 (Monochrome): Fomapan 200 (also sold as Fomapan 200 Creative) is a unique medium-speed black-and-white film from Foma Bohemia.
- Foma Fomapan 400 (Monochrome): Fomapan 400 is the high-speed member of Foma Bohemia's classic black-and-white film family. Using a traditional cubic-grain emulsion.
- Fuji Neopan 1600 (Monochrome): High-speed photojournalism film, punchy contrast, fine grain for its speed
- Fuji Neopan 400 (Monochrome): Versatile 400-speed, neutral gray balance, fine grain, workhorse film
- Fujifilm Acros (Monochrome): Virtually no reciprocity failure, ultra-fine grain, smooth highlight roll-off
- Gold Tone (Monochrome): Warm gold split-tone on grayscale, metallic midtone warmth, darkroom toning
- Ilford Delta 100 (Monochrome): Core-shell crystal technology, ultra-fine grain, smooth modern tonality
- Ilford Delta 3200 +2 (Monochrome): Pushed 2 stops (EI 12800), chunky golf-ball grain, extreme contrast
- Ilford Delta 3200 Microphen (Monochrome): Microphen developer variant, tighter grain for speed, boosted shadow detail
- Ilford Delta 3200 (Monochrome): A comprehensive analysis of the Ilford Delta 3200 visual signature — the "golf-ball grain, lifted blacks, low contrast.
- Ilford Delta 400 (Monochrome): Fine-grain 400-speed, modern T-grain emulsion, neutral tonal palette
- Ilford FP4 Plus 125 (Monochrome): Classic fine grain, rich creamy midtones, smooth highlight roll-off, 1935 heritage
- Ilford HP5 Plus +1 (Monochrome): Pushed 1 stop (EI 800), increased grain structure, punchier midtone contrast
- Ilford HP5 Plus +2 (Monochrome): Pushed 2 stops (EI 1600), pronounced grain, aggressive contrast, gritty texture
- Ilford HP5 Plus -1 (Monochrome): Pulled 1 stop (EI 200), reduced grain, compressed shadows, softer rendering
- Ilford HP5 Plus DD-X (Monochrome): Ilford DD-X developer, finer grain, more open shadow detail than ID-11 standard
- Ilford HP5 Plus Expired (Monochrome): Aged film stock, fogged emulsion base, reduced contrast, increased base grain
- Ilford HP5 Plus Stand Dev (Monochrome): 1-hour stand development with Rodinal, edge effects, compensating developer look
- Ilford HP5 Plus (Monochrome): A comprehensive breakdown of HP5's visual signature, with extended HP5 vs Tri-X analysis.
- Ilford MG Warmtone (Monochrome): Warm chlorobromide paper base, rich darkroom warmth, fiber-paper aesthetic
- Ilford Ortho Plus 80 (Monochrome): Blue/green sensitivity only, dark reds render black, high contrast, scientific film
- Ilford Pan F Plus 50 (Monochrome): Ultra-fine grain, high contrast, rich deep blacks, slowest Ilford emulsion
- Ilford SFX 200 (Monochrome): Extended red sensitivity, near-infrared effect with deep red/R72 filter
- Ilford XP2 Super (Monochrome): C-41 chromogenic film, dye-based grain, smooth highlights, flexible ISO
- Kentmere Pan 400 (Monochrome): Budget 400-speed, moderate grain, good midtone separation, entry-level classic
- Kodak Panatomic-X 32 (Monochrome): Kodak Panatomic-X was an ultra-fine-grain, slow-speed black-and-white negative film (ISO 32). Introduced in 1933 and discontinued in 1987.
- Kodak Plus-X 125 (Monochrome): Medium speed classic, fine grain, smooth creamy tonality, discontinued legend
- Kodak Recording Film 2475 (Monochrome): Kodak Recording Film 2475 was an ultra-high-speed black-and-white negative film designed for surveillance and law enforcement applications.
- Kodak T-Max 100 (Monochrome): T-grain micro-film, extremely fine grain, sharp acutance, modern rendering
- Kodak T-Max 3200 +2 (Monochrome): Pushed to EI 12800, heavy golf-ball grain, extreme contrast, concert staple
- Kodak T-Max 3200 (Monochrome): Ultra-high-speed multi-purpose, pronounced T-grain structure, dramatic tonality
- Kodak T-Max 400 (Monochrome): T-grain 400-speed, fine grain with enhanced sharpness, modern B&W alternative
- Kodak Technical Pan (Monochrome): Kodak Technical Pan (SO-115) was the highest-resolution black-and-white film ever commercially produced.
- Kodak Tri-X 400 +1 (Monochrome): Push +1 (EI 800), classic grain structure with bite, street photography grit
- Kodak Tri-X 400 +2 (Monochrome): Push +2 (EI 1600), aggressive grain, concert/low-light photojournalism staple
- Kodak Tri-X 400 -1 (Monochrome): Pulled 1 stop (EI 200), finer grain, compressed contrast, creamy rendering
- Kodak Tri-X 400 120 (Monochrome): Medium format version, finer apparent grain, smoother tonality at 6x6/6x7
- Kodak Tri-X 400 Expired (Monochrome): Aged emulsion, fogged base, reduced contrast, gritty vintage grain character
- Kodak Tri-X 400 HC-110 (Monochrome): HC-110 developer, tighter grain than D-76, more midtone bite and sharpness
- Kodak Tri-X 400 Rodinal (Monochrome): Rodinal developer, pronounced acutance, sharp grain edges, classic combo
- Kodak Tri-X 400 (Monochrome): The undisputed king of photojournalism B&W film. Distinctive grain pattern, crisp whites, aggressive mid-tones, legendary push behavior.
- Kodak Verichrome Pan (Monochrome): Kodak Verichrome Pan was a medium-speed black-and-white negative film designed for simple box cameras and consumer use.
- M645 Medium Format (Monochrome): Mamiya 645 aesthetic, finer apparent grain, creamy medium-format tonal scale
- Ricoh High-Contrast Monochrome (Monochrome): Heavy push-processing style, deep blacks, stark whites, aggressive street contrast
- Rollei Retro 400S (Monochrome): Rollei Retro 400S is a super-panchromatic 400-speed black-and-white film, the faster sibling of Retro 80S.
- Rollei Retro 80S (Monochrome): Rollei Retro 80S is a super-panchromatic (extended red sensitivity) fine-grain black-and-white film produced by Agfa-Gevaert (Belgium) and sold under the Rollei/Maco brand.
- Selenium Tone (Monochrome): Cool-purple black split-tone, archival darkroom selenium toning technique
- Sepia Tone (Monochrome): Warm brown classic darkroom toning, vintage print aesthetic, sulfide process
- Split Warm-Cool (Monochrome): Warm sepia highlights with cool selenium shadows, two-tone monochrome split

Slide / E-6 Film (20 presets)
Reversal film emulations: Kodachrome, Velvia, Provia, Astia, Ektachrome, Fortia, Sensia.

- AgfaChrome RS 100 (Color): German slide film, slightly warm/golden cast, moderate contrast. Agfa's professional reversal film with European color sensibility.
- Ektachrome 100G (Color): Predecessor to current E100, slightly warmer blue, finer grain. Professional standard for commercial work 2001-2012.
- Elite Chrome 200 (Color): Consumer-grade Ektachrome, warmer/more contrasty than pro E100, grainier. Kodak's affordable slide film for the mass market.
- Fuji Astia 100F (Color): Soft contrast portrait slide film, neutral skin tones, Fuji's wedding-workhorse reversal
- Fuji Fortia SP 50 (Color): Ultra-saturated limited edition slide, designed for cherry blossoms, Japan-only release
- Fuji Provia 100F (Color): Standard professional E-6 slide, neutral color balance, fine grain all-purpose workhorse
- Fuji Provia 400F (Color): Fuji Provia 400F (E-6, daylight balanced at 5500K) was Fujifilm's professional ISO 400 color transparency film, introduced as the second generation of the Provia 400 line.
- Fuji Provia 400X (Color): Fast 400-speed slide film, punchy saturation, surprisingly fine grain for speed
- Fuji Sensia 100 (Color): Consumer-grade Provia variant, slightly warmer rendering, good value E-6 film
- Fuji Velvia 100 (Color): Less extreme than Velvia 50, warmer, better skin tones. The most-used slide film by nature photographers in the 2000s.
- Fuji Velvia 50 (Color): The landscape photographer's holy grail. Extreme saturation, deep greens, punchy blues, crushed contrast, grain-free slide film perfection.
- Kodachrome 200 (Color): Higher-speed Kodachrome, warmer and grainier than K25/K64, good for sports/wildlife in the 1980s-90s.
- Kodachrome 25 (Color): Finest-grain slide film ever made (RMS 8), extremely sharp, slightly cooler than K64. Legendary among landscape photographers.
- Kodachrome 64 (Color): "Kodachrome had more poetry in it, a softness, an elegance. With digital photography, you gain many benefits [but] you have to put in post-production.
- Kodak Ektachrome 100VS (Color): Vivid Saturation variant, punchy reds and blues, pre-2009 landscape favorite
- Kodak Ektachrome 200 (Color): Kodak Ektachrome 200 (E-6, daylight balanced at 5500K) was Kodak's mid-speed professional slide film.
- Kodak Ektachrome 400X (Color): Kodak Ektachrome 400X (E-6, daylight balanced at 5500K) was Kodak's high-speed professional slide film.
- Kodak Ektachrome 64 (Color): Kodak Ektachrome 64 (E-6, daylight balanced at 5500K) was the mid-speed vintage Ektachrome slide film that predates the modern E100.
- Kodak Ektachrome E100 (Color): Modern E100 reissue, clean neutral slide rendering, fine grain everyday E-6 film
- Kodak Elite Chrome 400 (Color): Fast consumer-grade slide, punchy but grainy, Kodak's high-speed E-6 offering

Alternative Processes (25 presets)
Historic photographic processes: cyanotype, wet plate, daguerreotype, platinum, autochrome.

- Albumen Print (Monochrome): Glossy egg-white coated paper, warm brown-purple tones, 1850s Blanquart-Evrard
- Autochrome (Color): Pointillist potato-starch color grain, muted pastel palette, 1903 Lumière
- BW Infrared (Monochrome): White glowing foliage, black skies, near-IR spectral response, 720nm+ filter
- Bromoil (Monochrome): Bromide print inked with oil pigment, soft charcoal-like texture and brushwork
- Calotype (Monochrome): Paper negative aesthetic, soft detail, warm brown tones, 1841 Talbot patent
- Cross Process C41→E6 (Color): C-41 negative film in E-6 chemistry, high contrast with warm-orange shift
- Cross Process E6→C41 (Color): E-6 slide film developed in C-41 chemistry, strong green-blue color shift
- Cyanotype Classic (Monochrome): Prussian blue monochrome, high contrast, 1842 Sir John Herschel process
- Cyanotype Tea-Toned (Monochrome): Warm brown-toned cyanotype, split-toned blue/brown shadows via tannic acid
- Daguerreotype (Monochrome): Mirror-like polished silver plate, extremely fine detail, 1839 Daguerre
- Diana F+ (Color): Lo-fi 120 plastic camera, dreamy blur, vignetted square format, toy camera aesthetic
- Film Soup (Color): Boiled, dyed, or soaked negative — unpredictable color stains, warped texture
- Gum Bichromate (Color): Soft painterly texture, watercolor-like tonal gradations, pigment process
- Holga (Color): Plastic meniscus lens, heavy vignette, soft focus, light leaks, 120 medium format
- Lith Print (Monochrome): Infectious development, gritty grain, warm olive-yellow shadow tones
- Lomo LC-A (Color): High saturation, vignette-heavy, Minitar 32mm f/2.8 character, Lomography cult
- Palladium Print (Monochrome): Warmer than platinum, sepia-brown midtones, velvety deep shadows
- Pinhole (Color): Infinite depth of field, soft diffraction, long-exposure stillness, lensless photography
- Platinum Print (Monochrome): Matte finish, warm black-to-neutral tones, luminous highlight separation
- Redscale (Color): Red-orange-yellow color cast, reversed film layer shooting technique
- Salt Print (Monochrome): Matte paper, reddish-brown tones, 1830s Talbot calotype positive process
- Solarization (Monochrome): Partial tone reversal, dark Mackie-line halos around highlights, Man Ray style
- Van Dyke Brown (Monochrome): Deep chocolate brown, matte finish, iron-silver kallitype process
- Wet Plate Ambrotype (Monochrome): Positive image on glass backed with black, milky highlights, soft contrast
- Wet Plate Tintype (Monochrome): Positive image on blackened metal, brown-black tones, 1850s collodion

Photographer Styles (20 presets)
Signature styles of master photographers: Ansel Adams, Cartier-Bresson, McCurry, Eggleston.

- Alec Soth (Color): Honest, muted color: No color grading tricks. The color is what was there, rendered faithfully and quietly.
- Alex Webb (Color): Complex layered compositions: 3+ distinct planes of action in a single frame — each could be its own photograph
- Ansel Adams Zone System (Monochrome): Red filter skies: Dramatically darkened blue skies that separate clouds and mountain peaks. Blue channel pulled to near-black in the gray conversion.
- Cindy Sherman (Color): Film still aesthetic (Untitled Film Stills, 1977–1980): Black-and-white, but her color work carries the same DNA — as if they're production stills from movies that don't exist
- David LaChapelle (Color): Hyper-real saturation: Colors pushed beyond natural into a pop art dimension. Red is RED. Blue is BLUE.
- Fan Ho (Monochrome): Extreme geometric contrast: Backlit silhouettes against bright geometric light shafts
- Gregory Crewdson (Color): Cinematic teal/cool shadows: The defining color move. Shadows go blue/teal.
- Henri Cartier-Bresson (Monochrome): Moderate contrast: Not Ansel Adams dramatic, not flat. Natural tonal transitions.
- Joel Meyerowitz (Color): Cape Cod golden light: The defining characteristic of his later masterwork. Warm, hazy, almost tangible — light you can feel.
- Martin Parr (Color): Ring flash pop: Shadowless, flat lighting that saturates colors and eliminates depth. Like a specimen under a microscope.
- Michael Kenna (Monochrome): Long exposure smoothness: Water becomes mist, clouds become streaks, people vanish
- Nan Goldin (Color): Direct flash aesthetic: Hard shadows behind subjects, red-eye, blown highlights on faces — the snapshot turned art
- Peter Lindbergh (Monochrome): Lifted midtones: Blacks are never truly black. Shadows breathe. The entire image floats in Zone IV–VII.
- Saul Leiter (Color): Through-glass softness: Reflections on top of subjects, double exposures from window glass
- Sebastiao Salgado (Monochrome): Biblical luminance: Highlights that seem to glow from within. Zones VIII–IX placed deliberately.
- Steve McCurry (Color): Afghan Girl palette: Warm skin tones against cool/neutral backgrounds. The red-green contrast.
- Tim Walker (Color): Pastel palette: Lavender, mint, blush pink, butter yellow, powder blue — never saturated, always soft
- Todd Hido (Color): Cool blue/magenta night cast: The streetlight spectrum — sodium vapor (warm) mixed with fluorescent/LED (cool) creates distinctive magenta-blue shadows
- Vivian Maier (Monochrome): Square format aesthetic: Central compositions, balanced geometries
- William Eggleston (Color): Ordinary subjects, extraordinary color: A red ceiling, a blue tricycle, a green freezer — the color IS the subject
